transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

In class and in the hospital, I keep jumping in and answering or talking before people even finish their questions, and it’s getting me into serious trouble. I just can't seem to stop myself from interrupting my instructors and patients, and now I'm terrified I'm going to get kicked out of my training program.
Have you struggled with this impulsivity and interrupting others for most of your life, or is this a relatively new change that comes and goes alongside periods of unusually high energy?

This has actually been a lifelong pattern for me, ever since elementary school when teachers would send notes home about me blurting out answers and not waiting my turn. It's not something that comes and goes, but it has definitely become a major crisis recently because of the strict professional demands of my radiology program.
Do you also struggle with keeping your focus on tasks, organizing your work, or frequently making careless mistakes, even when you try your best to pay attention?

Honestly, I don't really struggle with focusing, organizing, or making careless mistakes on my work. My main issues are more about physical restlessness, impatience, and impulsively jumping into things or talking before I think. I just feel constantly revved up and have a really hard time slowing down.
Do you notice these same struggles with restlessness, impatience, or interrupting happening in your personal life as well, such as at home or when spending time with friends and family?

Yes, it absolutely affects my personal life too. Even when trying to relax and watch a movie with my family, I catch myself talking over the show, tapping my pen, or making noises because being quiet feels almost impossible. I feel like I'm constantly on the go from the moment I wake up until I go to sleep, never really taking a breather.
Have you been using any substances, such as high amounts of caffeine, energy drinks, or other stimulants, that might be causing or worsening this constant feeling of being revved up?

I don't really use stimulants or drink much caffeine at all, maybe just a soda once in a while. Besides, I've felt this exact same way since I was a little kid, long before I ever touched coffee or energy drinks.
Do you feel like this constant restlessness is driven by feelings of anxiety, worry, or nervousness, or is it more of a physical need to move that is present even when you feel calm and happy?

It's definitely more of a physical, internal drive to keep moving rather than anxiety or worry. Even when I'm trying to relax and do things I enjoy, like sketching or watching a movie, sitting still feels physically impossible and I have to fidget or make noise. A clinical preceptor actually pointed out to me that this lifelong "on the go" feeling seemed like a lot more than just nerves.

latest_inference.note: The patient exhibits a lifelong, cross-situational pattern of hyperactivity and impulsivity (blurting out answers, physical restlessness, inability to sit still, interrupting others) dating back to elementary school, which causes significant impairment in both professional and personal settings. She explicitly denies symptoms of inattention, and other differentials such as anxiety, substance use, and episodic mood disorders have been ruled out. Therefore, the diagnosis of Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive type (ICD-10-CM F90.1) is confirmed.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong history of prominent hyperactive and impulsive symptoms dating back to elementary school, which cause significant impairment in both professional (radiology program) and personal (home) settings. Specifically, the patient struggles with blurting out answers, interrupting others, physical restlessness, and feeling constantly 'on the go.' The patient explicitly denies significant difficulties with inattention, organization, or careless mistakes, pointing to a predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation. The symptoms are not better explained by anxiety, other mental disorders, or substance use.
